claims.text: Transabdominal ultrasound is the best test to detect gallstones; it may also elicit tenderness over the gallbladder (ultrasonographic Murphy sign); pericholecystic fluid or gallbladder wall thickening indicates acute inflammation
claims.quote: Transabdominal ultrasound is the best test to detect gallstones. The test may also elicit local abdominal tenderness over the gallbladder (ultrasonographic Murphy sign). Pericholecystic fluid or thickening of the gallbladder wall indicates acute inflammation.

claims.text: HIDA scan: the gallbladder normally visualizes within 30-60 min; non-visualization at 1-4 h = acute cholecystitis; EF <35-40% → chronic cholecystitis / biliary dyskinesia; use when US is equivocal but suspicion remains

claims.text: Cholescintigraphy is useful when results are equivocal: failure of the radionuclide to fill the gallbladder suggests an obstructed cystic duct; false positives can come from critical illness, parenteral nutrition, severe liver disease or previous sphincterotomy
claims.quote: Cholescintigraphy is useful when results are equivocal; failure of the radionuclide to fill the gallbladder suggests an obstructed cystic duct (ie, an impacted stone). The use of cholescintigraphy is sometimes limited due to practical considerations, particularly in patients with hemodynamic instability (eg, in the intensive care unit) who cannot be transported and tolerate the scan duration. False-positive results may be due to the following: A critical illness Parenteral nutrition (because gallbladder stasis prevents filling) Severe liver disease (because the liver does not secrete the radionuclide) Previous sphincterotomy (which facilitates flow into the duodenum rather than the gallbladder)

claims.text: Abdominal CT and MRI identify complications such as gallbladder perforation or pancreatitis, as well as choledocholithiasis
claims.quote: Abdominal CT and MRI identify complications such as gallbladder perforation or pancreatitis, as well as choledocholithiasis and other extrabiliary involvement.

claims.text: Labs are not diagnostic: leukocytosis with a left shift is common; liver tests are normal or only slightly elevated in uncomplicated disease
claims.quote: Laboratory tests are performed but are not diagnostic. Leukocytosis with a left shift is common. In uncomplicated acute cholecystitis, liver tests are normal or only slightly elevated.

claims.text: Causes The most common complication of cholelithiasis (≥ 90% have gallstones): a stone impacted in the cystic duct persistently obstructs it → acute inflammation; bile stasis triggers release of inflammatory enzymes
claims.quote: Acute cholecystitis is the most common complication of cholelithiasis. In fact, ≥ 90% of patients with acute cholecystitis have cholelithiasis (1). When a stone becomes impacted in the cystic duct and persistently obstructs it, acute inflammation results. Bile stasis triggers release of inflammatory enzymes (eg, phospholipase A, which converts lecithin to lysolecithin, which then may mediate inflammation).

claims.text: The mucosa secretes more fluid than it absorbs; distention releases more mediators, worsening mucosal damage and causing ischemia; bacterial infection can supervene; unchecked, it can lead to necrosis and perforation
claims.quote: The damaged mucosa secretes more fluid into the gallbladder lumen than it absorbs. The resulting distention further releases inflammatory mediators (eg, prostaglandins), worsening mucosal damage and causing ischemia, all of which perpetuate inflammation. Bacterial infection can supervene. The vicious circle of fluid secretion and inflammation, when unchecked, can lead to necrosis and perforation.

claims.text: Symptoms Pain like biliary colic but longer (> 6 hours) and more severe; vomiting and right subcostal tenderness are common; pain may be referred to the right scapula; within a few hours the Murphy sign develops with right upper guarding; fever, usually low grade, is common
claims.quote: Most patients have had prior attacks of biliary colic or acute cholecystitis. The pain of cholecystitis is similar in quality and location to biliary colic but lasts longer (peaking within 15 to 60 minutes and lasting > 6 hours) and is more severe. Vomiting is common, as is right subcostal tenderness. Pain may be referred to the right scapula or upper back. Within a few hours, the Murphy sign (deep inspiration exacerbates the pain during palpation of the right upper quadrant and halts inspiration) develops along with involuntary guarding of upper abdominal muscles on the right side. Fever, usually low grade, is common.

claims.text: Older patients: the first or only symptoms may be systemic and nonspecific (eg, anorexia, vomiting, malaise, weakness, fever); sometimes no fever develops
claims.quote: In older patients, the first or only symptoms may be systemic and nonspecific (eg, anorexia, vomiting, malaise, weakness, fever). Sometimes fever does not develop.

claims.text: Without treatment, approximately 10% may develop perforation and peritonitis (perforated gallbladder mortality up to 16%); increasing pain, high fever and rigors with rebound tenderness or ileus suggest empyema, gangrene or perforation
claims.quote: Without treatment, approximately 10% of patients may develop localized or free perforation and peritonitis (2). Perforated gallbladder has a mortality rate of up to 16%. Increasing abdominal pain, high fever, and rigors with rebound tenderness or ileus suggest empyema (pus) in the gallbladder, gangrene, or perforation.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: NPO, IV antibiotics, cholecystectomy

claims.text: Admit for IV fluids and analgesics (an NSAID such as ketorolac, or an opioid); nothing by mouth, NG suction if vomiting or ileus; parenteral antibiotics are usually started (eg, ampicillin/sulbactam or piperacillin/tazobactam), though benefit is lacking in mild disease
claims.quote: Management includes hospital admission, IV fluids, and analgesics (eg, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug ([NSAID] such as ketorolac or an opioid). Nothing is given orally, and nasogastric suction is instituted if vomiting or an ileus is present. Parenteral antibiotics are usually initiated to treat possible infection, but evidence of benefit is lacking in cases of mild acute cholecystitis (1). Empiric coverage, directed at gram-negative enteric organisms, involves IV regimens such as ampicillin/sulbactam or piperacillin/tazobactam (2).

claims.text: Early cholecystectomy is favored over conservative management; it cures acute cholecystitis and is recommended within 7 days of admission and within 10 days of symptom onset
claims.quote: While resolution without surgery can occur, early cholecystectomy is favored over conservative management given the relatively high rates of complication and recurrence. Cholecystectomy cures acute cholecystitis and relieves biliary pain. Cholecystectomy for both calculous and acalculous cholecystitis is recommended within 7 days of hospital admission and within 10 days of the onset of symptoms (1).

claims.text: Cholecystectomy is usually laparoscopic; open surgery may be done for technical difficulty or severe inflammation
claims.quote: Cholecystectomy is usually performed laparoscopically, although open cholecystectomy may be performed in cases of technical difficulty or severe inflammation (1).
